meaning: Driving a robot by hand; on the SO-101 a person moves a leader arm and the follower arm copies it.
The arm a person holds and moves; its motors are off and only its joint angles are read.
The arm that receives the leader's joint angles as targets and does the task; the robot in this dive.
The laptop or small board the arm and cameras plug into by USB, which runs the control loop.
Everything the robot knows at one instant: on the SO-101, six joint angles plus one image per camera.
A sensor on a joint that reports its angle as a whole number of steps, 4096 per turn on the SO-101.
A robot's sense of its own body; on the SO-101 it is the six joint angles.
Recording each joint's range once so that raw encoder steps map to the same scale on every arm.
What the robot is told to do at one instant: on the SO-101, six target joint angles.
The trained model that picks the action from the observation.
A motor, gearbox, encoder and microcontroller in one box that holds the angle it was last told.
The program inside a servo that compares the measured angle with the goal angle and drives the motor to close the gap.
A tuning number of a controller that sets how strongly it reacts to the error.
A controller that sets the motor drive from the error now (P), its sum over time (I) and how fast it is changing (D).
A PID controller with the integral term off: it pushes in proportion to the error and brakes when the error shrinks fast.
One independent way a mechanism can move; each rotary joint of the arm adds one.
The tool at the end of the arm; on the SO-101, the gripper.
Stating an action as one target angle per motor.
Stating an action as the position and orientation of the gripper, which software then converts to joint angles.
Computing the joint angles that put the gripper at a wanted position and orientation.
A file describing the arm's link lengths and joint axes, needed to convert between gripper poses and joint angles.
An action whose numbers are the targets themselves.
An action given as an offset from the robot's state at the moment the policy made its prediction.
An action given as an offset from the previous action, so errors add up along the sequence.
One cycle of the host loop: read sensors, decide, write goals, sleep until the next cycle is due.
The number of ticks per second; 30 Hz, or 33.3 ms per tick, when LeRobot records.
Times per second.
Several future actions returned by one policy call, which the host plays one per tick.
The stack of loops on a robot, each slower and doing more thinking than the one below: servo loop, host loop, policy, planner.
A slower loop that decides what to do next and hands targets to a faster controller.
A faster, simpler loop that tracks the targets a planner or policy gives it.
On a humanoid, a small network that turns the plan into joint targets many times a second.
A robot with two legs and two arms.
Free play in a gear train that lets the joint move without the motor turning; up to 0.5 degrees on the SO-101's servo.
A policy built on a network that takes camera images and a text instruction and outputs actions.
NVIDIA's line of onboard computers for robots; the AGX Thor and the Orin are two of them.
A recording of a person doing the task through the robot, stored as observations and the six target angles the person's hand asked for.
The single data line the six servos share with the host, on which each servo answers by its ID.
The length of one tick: 33.3 ms at 30 Hz.
A run in which a trained policy, and no person, drives the arm.
Running the policy inside the control loop, which blocks until the action is computed, so the arm stops during each call.
Computing the following action chunk in a background thread while the loop plays the current one, for a model too slow to answer inside a tick.
Running the policy on a server on another machine while the host beside the arm keeps the cameras and the motors.
LeRobot's timing summary of a session: time per step of the loop and the time slept per tick.
NVIDIA's inference runtime, which compiles a model for a given GPU.
